title: Assembly foundation and maintainability
outcome: A new maintainer or coding agent can change frame.asm safely using explicit NASM structure, ABI, style, review, and optimization contracts.
baseline: frame is a large single-file freestanding NASM server with valuable inline history but no previously enforced repository-wide assembly or agent contract.
nonGoals: A language rewrite, speculative instruction tuning, or splitting code before ownership and protocol boundaries are measured.
acceptance: Assembly structure, naming, syscall, wire-layout, cleanup, and optimization rules are versioned and linted.
Agent instructions agree across Codex, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and repository-local scopes.
Low-level optimization changes require repeatable measurements and regression evidence.

title: Layered protocol and regression test system
outcome: Every supported protocol and safety contract has a deterministic lowest-layer test, with malformed clients isolated from the server and other clients.
baseline: The original repository relied primarily on manual execution and lacked a manifest connecting unit, integration, regression, fuzz, reproducibility, and hardware acceptance lanes.
nonGoals: Opening DRM, evdev, KVM, or a live user display in ordinary tests or turning noisy performance numbers into PR gates.
acceptance: Unit, static, headless integration, regression, malformed-input, reproducibility, and manual-hardware lanes are documented and runnable.
Every repaired defect gains a named regression and every server test proves socket/process cleanup.
The test manifest records ownership, hardware boundaries, commands, and implementation status.

title: Secure CI, SonarQube, packaging, and release provenance
outcome: Pull requests are read-only and reproducibly gated, while trusted releases produce scanned, signed, traceable native packages and OCI images without exposing infrastructure secrets.
baseline: The source built locally but had no versioned hooks, hosted/self-hosted trust split, secret history scan, Sonar assembly policy, SBOM, image, ECR, or provenance workflow.
nonGoals: Publishing from pull requests, sharing a host Docker socket, running privileged CI, or enabling ECR/Sonar/self-hosted jobs before their external resources are ready.
acceptance: CI/CD/RO workflows, local hooks, runner safety checks, and quality gates are versioned and pinned.
git-secrets, Gitleaks, GitHub push protection, dependency review, and binary security scans run at the appropriate trust boundary.
SemVer tags produce checksums, SBOMs, OCI artifacts, scans, attestations, and approval-gated delivery.

title: X11 core protocol conformance
outcome: Supported core X11 requests, replies, errors, events, byte lengths, and sequence behavior match xorgproto and canonical X.Org semantics.
baseline: frame implements a broad core subset, but handlers need a request-by-request conformance inventory and consistent malformed-stream behavior.
nonGoals: Claiming full X11 conformance for unimplemented requests or adding isolated swapped-client behavior without an end-to-end design.
acceptance: A machine-readable core opcode matrix records support, semantics, tests, and deliberate incompatibilities.
Every implemented variable-length request validates exact bounds and preserves client stream framing.
Replies, errors, events, and sequence numbers match canonical protocol evidence.

title: Multi-client resource ownership and lifecycle
outcome: Windows, pixmaps, GCs, fonts, cursors, selections, grabs, subscriptions, and extension state are isolated by client and reclaimed deterministically.
baseline: Resource tables and disconnect paths exist, but each owner, capacity, cascade, and slot-reuse invariant needs explicit proof.
nonGoals: Increasing fixed table sizes as a substitute for ownership, bounds, cleanup, or denial-of-service analysis.
acceptance: Every resource type documents creation ownership, lookup authorization, dependency cascades, capacity failure, and disconnect cleanup.
Cross-client misuse returns a bounded protocol failure without corrupting either client.
Slot reuse is regression-tested with clean state after disconnect.

title: Rendering and compositor correctness
outcome: Core drawing, RENDER operations, backing storage, exposure, damage, stacking, and composition produce deterministic pixels with measured cost.
baseline: The software compositor can display representative clients, but drawing semantics and repaint granularity remain uneven and active text workloads expose a memory-bandwidth hotspot.
nonGoals: Optimizing away protocol correctness, hiding unsupported operators, or gating ordinary PRs on workstation timing noise.
acceptance: Pixel-exact fixtures cover supported core and RENDER operations, clipping, overlap, alpha, and bounds.
Damage/exposure/stacking behavior is regression-tested across mapped window trees.
Representative workloads have repeatable CPU, memory, syscall, wakeup, and compositor-counter baselines.

title: Synthetic input and XKB compatibility
milestone: v0.4.0 - Input, XKB, and extension interoperability
outcome: Pointer, keyboard, focus, grabs, synthetic input, and XKB state support interactive desktop use without opening live input devices in automation.
baseline: Core and extension input paths exist, while Firefox-class XKB compatibility and a complete synthetic interaction matrix remain unfinished.
nonGoals: Reading /dev/input in CI, requiring root, or treating one US-layout happy path as XKB conformance.
acceptance: A FIFO/socket-driven synthetic harness covers key, button, motion, focus, grab, drag, and resize flows.
XKB discovery, maps, state, events, and multiple representative layouts interoperate with toolkit clients.
Live evdev behavior is isolated to the manual hardware milestone.

title: Extension interoperability and conformance
milestone: v0.4.0 - Input, XKB, and extension interoperability
outcome: Advertised X11 extensions expose internally consistent versions, request sets, events, errors, resources, and cleanup behavior required by representative clients.
baseline: frame advertises several extensions, but toolkit probes and real-client traces still encounter partial request families and placeholder semantics.
nonGoals: Advertising extensions or versions that the server cannot safely service, or implementing unused surface area without trace/test evidence.
acceptance: An extension matrix records advertised versions, opcodes, events, errors, clients, tests, and unsupported boundaries.
Toolkit and representative-client startup traces contain no reply-bearing deadlocks or stream desynchronization.
Extension resources and subscriptions are client-owned and reclaimed.

title: DRM, evdev, hotplug, and recovery
outcome: A human can start, switch away from, hotplug, interrupt, and stop frame on supported hardware without wedging input, DRM master, scanout, or the subsequent display server.
baseline: DRM/KMS and evdev paths are present and documented, but hardware acceptance must be repeated on controlled TTYs with explicit recovery evidence.
nonGoals: Autonomous hardware testing, privileged CI, opening live devices from hooks, or accepting a result without restore/recovery proof.
acceptance: Every acquisition stage has signal/error cleanup and reverse-order restoration evidence.
Single/multi-output, page flip, VT switch, hotplug, device loss, and input unplug cases are manually recorded.
The original console/display server starts cleanly after every acceptance run.

title: Representative desktop and client compatibility
outcome: tswm, terminals, Firefox, and the declared representative client set are visually correct, interactive, recoverable, and measured on frame.
baseline: tswm and xterm now reach a visible prompt through the headless compositor after implementing key core requests, while Firefox, complete interaction flows, and bare-console performance acceptance remain open.
nonGoals: Calling a client supported because its first window maps, or presenting nested/headless benchmark numbers as bare-metal Xorg results.
acceptance: tswm and xterm reach visual and interaction parity for the declared baseline session.
Firefox launches a local test profile and supports focus, move, resize, keyboard, pointer, close, and sustained rendering.
Matched control/frame sessions have reproducible performance evidence and explicit compatibility limitations.
